entries.title: Shot clock controls, break time, and tidier panels
entries.body: The shot clock panel on the desktop now has its own on/off button, a Pause/Resume button, and dials for per-shot seconds and time after the break - the app spots a break automatically (five or more balls scattering) and gives the next shot the longer countdown. The Stats and Shot Timeline panels now collapse like the others, so you can fold away what you're not using.
details: Pause freezes the countdown and its sounds; Resume continues from the same number.
The clock panel stays visible even when the clock is off, since that's where the on/off lives now.

entries.title: Shot clock is live, plus a menu bar and a squishable window
entries.body: The shot clock now runs off the cue ball itself: the countdown starts the moment your cue ball stops rolling and stops the instant you strike it. Sounds mark every phase - a rising cue when the clock starts (including after every shot), a warning beep, 3-2-1 ticks, and the buzzer. It works with or without recording, and you can flip it on and off from the new Play menu. The desktop window also squishes down to about a third of the screen now, and a File menu keeps everything reachable when it's narrow.
details: Clock settings (seconds, warning time, sounds) are in Settings > Shot clock; the Play menu is just the on/off.
The countdown starts about a fifth of a second after the cue ball truly rests - that debounce is what stops table jitter from false-starting the clock.
Next precision step when it matters: using the strike SOUND to stop the clock frame-exactly.

entries.title: Stay-down timer on the desktop scoreboard
entries.body: The timer you asked for: a STAY-DOWN row on the live scoreboard. It starts counting the moment you take the shot (shown with a ~ while it's a live estimate), then locks to the camera-measured number seconds later - green when you stayed down, red POP when you popped up early. If the camera couldn't measure that shot, it shows a dash instead of guessing.
details: Counts only while recording, same as the rest of the scoreboard.
The live count is an estimate; the locked number is the same measured stay-down you see in shot details.

entries.title: Clips load and play much lighter
entries.body: Every session now gets a lightweight playback copy made right after it ends - about a fifth the data of the original. Your phone picks it automatically, so clips start faster, scrub smoother, and use far less cellular data. Same video, same overlays, same everything - just easier for the phone to play. This is also the leading fix for the tail stutter: the originals were heavy enough to strain the phone's video decoder.
details: The lightweight copies match the originals frame-for-frame, so trails, aim lines and shot times line up exactly.
Older sessions are being converted in the background; each one switches over as soon as its copy is ready.
Recording always comes first: any conversion stops instantly the moment a session starts.

entries.title: Full-length ball trails, no more circle
entries.body: The tails now cover the entire shot - strike to rest - for the cue AND object balls, across the whole library. Two data bugs were cutting them short: the sampling window opened after the ball had already covered most of its travel, and the tracker's number-dropping during fast flight filtered out the flight itself. Both fixed; the circle covering the ball is gone too.
details: Proof case: a marathon-session shot whose tail was the last foot now draws the full 582-pixel strike-to-rest path.
Unnumbered fast-flight stretches inherit the ball's identity only when the track's numbered segments on both sides agree - the old protection against mid-flight identity mixups stays intact.

For the remaining lag/stutter: triple-tap the top bar in the player for a live diagnostics readout, and send a screenshot of it during a stutter - it will show whether the phone is dropping video frames on these high-bitrate files.

entries.title: Miss analysis caught up on every session
entries.body: A gap in the pipeline meant new sessions weren't getting the deep second-pass that resolves tricky misses - your marathon session had 51 misses and only 1 categorized. That pass now runs automatically at every session close, and the whole library was swept: 180 verdicts recovered, trusted tags 150 -> 227, uncategorized 203 -> 126. Your Lifetime Stats patterns just got a lot more data behind them.
details: Found via the abstention notes shipped last week: 48 marathon misses stated their reasons, and the reasons pointed at the missing pipeline stage rather than bad tracking.
The remaining 126 uncategorized are genuine hard cases (each states why) - your grading playlists can settle any of them with two taps.
The drift tests now require this stage in the close pass, so it can never silently fall out again.

entries.title: The 9-ball mixup is fixed — 100% on gameplay footage
entries.body: The washed-out-9 problem's last remnant is gone. A correction layer tuned for the OLD camera settings was flipping the 9 into the 1 (nine times out of fifteen on real gameplay frames) even though the AI model itself read every single one correctly. That layer now only upgrades, never downgrades - and ball identification on gameplay frames from your last two sessions measures 100% across every ball on the table.
details: Found by building hand-verified ground truth from your own gameplay (12 layouts across the two Aug-24 evening sessions), then testing each pipeline layer separately: the model scored 15/15 on true 9s; the correction layer was the corruptor.
The fix was checked on three frame sets before shipping - gameplay (100% overall), dense racks (slightly better), and old-era archives (net neutral).
Three new tests guard it, including 'a model stripe answer must never be demoted'.

entries.title: The shot Details sheet got a real design
entries.body: You called it the worst UI you'd ever seen - fair. It's now a proper bottom sheet: slides over the player instead of shoving the page under the clock, groups MEASURED data apart from YOUR CALL verdicts, shrinks the utility buttons to an icon row, and pins Cancel / Looks right / Save to a fixed footer. Your stay-down time shows as a big readout at the top of MEASURED - with a POPPED EARLY flag when it applies.
details: Selected verdict buttons now fill solid green instead of a thin outline tint.
The abstention notes (why an aim line or metric is absent) sit inside the MEASURED group where they belong.
Tap the dimmed backdrop to close - same as Cancel.
This is the first slice of the phase-3 UI pass; the player itself is next.

entries.title: New ball-ID model promoted: 18% fewer misreads
entries.body: The challenger trained on the newly-mined layouts beat the champion on strictly held-out sessions - 18% fewer out-of-game number claims with coverage unchanged - and is now live. It's the first promotion since c5, and the first payoff from unblocking the layout miner.
details: Judged fairly: identical 24 sessions for both models, every session that contributed training data excluded, so the win can't be memorization.
The old champion is archived one copy away for instant rollback.
Next accuracy lever: the starved stripe balls (10 and 12 still have one training example each) - one minute of a racked 8-ball game on camera feeds them automatically now.

entries.title: Found it: one clock bug behind everything tonight
entries.body: The analysis clock ran ~3 seconds behind the video - every symptom you hit inherited it. Trails animated seconds after the balls had stopped. Aim lines were computed on mid-shot frames (wrong line, or no line at all). Slow-mo clips cut at the skewed time and started mid-shot. All timestamps are now anchored to the video itself, per shot, using each shot's frame-verified strike moment.
details: Your @58 shot now has its aim line. Tonight's session re-verified server-side: shot 3's line lies exactly along the stick, through the cue ball, stopping at the 4.
The jittery move-stop-move tail is fixed too (the overlay clock could step backwards between frames; it can't now).
Tonight's session is fully corrected; the rest of the library retrofits overnight.
This is phase 1 of the cleanup you called for. Phase 2 makes every shot go through ONE identical pipeline the moment it completes - no more some-shots-analyzed-some-not. Phase 3 is the UI redesign.

entries.title: Trails and aim lines stay glued to the right shot
entries.body: You caught it exactly: during laggy loads, the overlay clock kept running from the previous position, so the previous shot's (perfectly drawn) trail animated over the wrong footage - and aim lines could show for a shot the picture hadn't reached yet. The player now refuses to draw any overlay while the picture can't match it, and every navigation resets the overlay clock.
details: Root cause 1: jumping between shots bypassed the overlay clock's reset, so during a slow seek it extrapolated from the old position - the old trail kept animating until the new shot's first frame arrived.
Root cause 2: in playlists that hop between session videos, a cached trail from the same shot NUMBER in the previous session could be reused. The cache now knows which session it belongs to.
New rule everywhere: mid-seek, mid-load, or mid-swap, the overlay layer goes blank instead of guessing - same philosophy as detection's 'show nothing rather than something wrong'.

An adversarial review of the whole overlay timing system also caught and fixed: stale scrub seeks replaying after navigation, the frame-scrubber serving another session's cached frames after a playlist hop, and background frame-warming making overlays flicker while paused.

entries.title: You were right: quick pop-ups go with misses
entries.body: Overnight, every shot in the library (1,193 across 35 sessions) got its stroke measured. The pattern you predicted is real: 32% of your misses come with a stay-down under 1 second, versus 16% of your makes - exactly double. Your median hold is also 0.3s shorter on misses (1.27s vs 1.57s). Lifetime Stats now shows medians and quick-exit rates.
details: The averages almost hid this (1.58s vs 1.65s) - the signature is a fat tail of quick exits on misses, so the stats show median and %-under-1-second instead.
No shot in the library measured under 0.7s, so your 'pop-ups' are subtle - a 0.9s exit, not a jump. The camera catches what feels invisible.
Every shot's Details sheet now carries its own numbers - check a few of your misses against your makes.

entries.title: New metric: how long you stay down on the shot
entries.body: Every shot now gets stroke measurements straight from the camera: how long your cue stays down after contact, your backstroke length, the pause at the top of it, and your practice-stroke count. Misses often come with popping up early - now there's a number for it, and Lifetime Stats compares your average stay-down on makes vs misses.
details: Verified frame-by-frame before shipping: 9 of 9 measured shots matched hand-checked ground truth within 0.1 seconds (a tenth shot, where the balls were moved by hand, correctly measured nothing).
The shot Details sheet shows a STROKE row: stay-down seconds, an early pop-up warning, pause milliseconds, backstroke length, practice strokes.
Under the hood the true strike moment is re-detected from the cue ball's disappearance (the tracker's shot clock runs ~2.4s late), and the cue stick is tracked even when your arm overlaps it.
These field names match your Bluetooth cue sensor's - when it's installed, both sources will measure the same things and check each other.

entries.title: Tracking sees through the grain now
entries.body: Tonight's high-ISO footage was confusing the ball tracker (identity mix-ups ran 4x the usual rate). The analysis feed now gets cleaned of grain before the detector looks at it - measured on your grainiest session: fewer identity mix-ups, better ball numbering, and 12-13% more balls held per frame. Your recordings are untouched.
details: Verified on two separate 6-minute slices before enabling: identity hops down 15%, ball-number coverage up, track fragmentation down 14-21%, and more balls tracked per frame in both tests with no metric worse.
This is the software half of the grain fix. The camera half (1/250 shutter + half the ISO next time you're at the rig) removes grain at the source and roughly halves file sizes too.

entries.title: Trail animations keep up with the ball now
entries.body: The animated trails lagged because the phone's browser reports video time slightly in the past, and three hidden per-frame costs were eating the iPhone's processing budget. The overlay now reads the exact time of each displayed frame, and those costs are gone.
details: The overlay clock now uses frame callbacks (exact presented-frame timestamps, iOS 15.4+) instead of the stale 'official playback position', with a clean fallback when paused or on older devices. This also fixes extra lag in Low Power Mode.

The frame cache that makes scrubbing instant was JPEG-encoding every single frame during playback; it now stores every 3rd frame (scrubbing still always hits, and the cache covers 70 seconds instead of 23).
Two canvas layers were being reallocated on every animation tick even when nothing was drawn - both now only rebuild when the size actually changes.

entries.title: Clips now start instantly on your phone
entries.body: Every recording had its seek index at the wrong end of the file, so your phone had to download huge chunks (up to ~2 GB for a late shot in a long session) before it could play anything. The index now sits at the front: playing any shot needs ~5-10 MB. All 26 older recordings were fixed tonight, and every new recording fixes itself automatically.
details: The recorder writes 'fragmented' video on purpose - it means a crash can't destroy a recording mid-write. But fragmented files carry an empty index up front; iOS can't even learn the clip's duration from it, let alone jump to a shot, so Safari crawled the file from the beginning.

The fix re-containers the finished file (a pure copy, ~1.4 seconds per GB, no quality change) right after recording stops - before it ever reaches Dropbox. Crash safety is unchanged: the file stays fragmented while recording is live.
Also found: tonight's high-ISO settings inflate file bitrate 4.6x (16 Mbps vs 3.5), which multiplies every download. The grain recommendation coming separately addresses this too.

entries.title: You were right about the shutter — blur is fixed
entries.body: The new camera settings are real and working: a crop of the fastest-moving thing in your latest clip (the cue stick mid-stroke) is tack sharp. My earlier claim that the shutter 'wasn't applying' was my measurement's fault — it was counting pieces of your cue stick as blurred balls.
details: The smear detector ranks elongated blobs, and a cue stick is naturally elongated — no motion needed. Once your 1/500 shutter made the balls crisp, stick fragments were the only stretched shapes left, and they topped the list looking like blur.
The decisive test: the fastest mover in session 18:55 (inter-frame extent 199px — full stroke speed) shows zero smear in a single frame. At the old 1/60 exposure it would have smeared ~75px.

What this unlocks: fast shots stop vanishing mid-flight. 39 of the 62 remaining uncategorized misses failed because the ball was never captured between strike and pocket — that failure class should not exist in new recordings.

entries.title: Fixed the laggy mouse and keyboard
entries.body: The AI was hogging the graphics chip — the same chip Windows uses to draw your cursor and keystrokes, which is why typing felt broken whenever the app ran. Ball detection now runs on the CPU instead: your desktop got its graphics chip back (app's share: 69% → 0%), and detection barely slows down.
details: Root cause: DirectML inference saturated the Radeon 780M's 3D engine at ~30 inferences/sec. On an integrated GPU that's the exact engine the Windows compositor needs for the cursor, and GPU engines have no preemptive priority — which is why every process/thread priority fix failed to help.

Measured before choosing: CPU at 4 threads does a full tiled detection in 88ms (~11/sec) vs ~15/sec on the GPU. Detections verified identical between the two (6/6 balls matched within 2px, same numbers).

It's a setting (detection.inference_provider: auto/gpu/cpu), so a future camera-PC or GPU upgrade flips it back with one word. The CPU session is capped at 4 threads and the app runs below-normal priority, so your input always preempts it.

entries.title: 31 more misses solved — backlog down to 62
entries.body: A smarter read of rattle-heavy shots (judging only the ball's initial run, not the chaos after it hits the jaws) solved 31 more misses. Trusted verdicts: 116 → 147. Uncategorized: 93 → 62.
details: A measurement pass showed most stuck shots weren't missing data — they were fully observed but their paths bend too much (rattles, rebounds) for a whole-journey fit. The verdict only ever needed the first straight run from contact, so that's what gets judged now, under an even stricter straightness bar.

Of the 62 remaining: 39 were never captured at all (the shutter-speed change will prevent these going forward), 21 are genuinely too messy to trust, 2 pointed at no pocket. All stay in your grading playlist rather than being guessed.
Your categorized misses now split about even left/right overall — with 'cut right, missed right' (overcut) still the single biggest bucket at 28.

entries.title: 77 backlog misses solved automatically
entries.body: The forensic solver you pushed for went through the uncategorized pile: 77 of 171 misses now carry a verdict (Uncategorized 171 → 94, trusted verdicts 38 → 115). Your own corrections still outrank everything.
details: It re-opens only the blurry second of each miss and searches the narrow corridor physics allows, matched against that ball's own colour — about 8 minutes of compute for the whole pile, versus the 13-hour full rerun that measurably didn't work.
Interesting early signal: the newly solved misses split 36 left / 41 right — much more balanced than the first trusted batch suggested. Worth watching as the rest get graded.

Honestly held back: 54 shots where the fit wasn't trustworthy and 39 where the ball's flight was never captured at all — those stay in your grading queue rather than being guessed. 49 solved shots know the miss side but not the cut (the cue wasn't tracked); they're listed as 'cut unknown' and count toward totals.

entries.title: Miss verdicts now come from physics
entries.body: Every clip's miss side is now read off a physics fit of the ball's whole path — the method that got both hand-verified shots right, including one the old approach called confidently wrong. Trusted misses grew 33 → 38 and the table updated.
details: The old approach judged direction from a few samples near the pocket, which a rattle could fool — your 4-ball shot and one other verified clip proved it. The new approach fits straight rolling legs to every observation of the ball and reads the verdict off the fit, with its own error bar deciding when to trust it.
Your grading queue (Uncategorized) still works exactly the same — and every verdict you enter keeps training the system's honesty checks.

entries.title: Tap a stats line to grade those clips
entries.body: Every miss subgenre in Lifetime Stats — including Uncategorized — is now a playlist. Tap it, watch the clips, and set Cut/Missed in each shot's Details. Grading an Uncategorized miss moves it into its subgenre and sharpens the table.

entries.title: Stats restructured your way
entries.body: Lifetime Stats now reads top-down: Total Shots, Makes, Misses — then each miss subgenre with its meaning built in: Cut Left / Miss Left (Overcut), Cut Left / Miss Right (Undercut), and so on.

entries.title: What's New and Stats actually open now
entries.body: Both are full pages with a ‹ Home button, not pop-ups — and the bug where tapping them did nothing until you opened a session is fixed (they were opening inside a hidden layer).

entries.title: Lifetime Stats — and your verdicts now count
entries.body: New on the home screen: Lifetime Stats, a tight table of your misses — Cut Left/Straight/Right against Missed Left/Right. And in any shot's Details you can now set Cut and Missed yourself; your word overrides the machine and feeds the table.
details: Only trusted verdicts are counted: shots the analysis saw clearly, plus anything you've corrected by hand. Shots where the ball was lost stay out of the table rather than polluting it.
Your corrections do double duty: they fix the record, and they become the ground truth that validates the physics-fit work — every verdict you enter makes the automatic tagging measurably better.

entries.title: Player restored
entries.body: The chrome-free player experiment is rolled back — the clips screen is exactly as it was. The Instagram-style redesign is shelved for another day.

entries.title: Home screen restored
entries.body: The card list is gone — the home screen is back to the layout you didn't mind (What's New row stays, pause-fade stays). The real redesign target is the clips player, Instagram-style, coming next.

entries.title: Pause button gets out of the way
entries.body: The play symbol now fades out a moment after you pause, so it no longer sits on top of the frame you paused to study.

entries.title: What's New moved home
entries.body: This panel now lives at the top of the home screen, where it belongs — the menu inside the player is back to being just overlays and drawing tools.
details: Fair catch: the update feed had been tucked into the player's drawing menu, which made no sense. It's now a single row above your sessions — latest headline visible, dot when there's something unread, tap to read.
A broader cleanup of the sessions screen is queued next.

entries.title: Your disputed shot now reads correctly
entries.body: The 4-ball at 3:52 now shows 'missed left, 1.3 inches' with full confidence — matching what you saw. The same check was applied to every clip.
details: When you flagged the shot at 3:52 ('this should be a pretty clear miss left'), the app said the opposite. Getting it right ended up fixing four separate problems, and each one is now better for every clip in your library.

First: the camera. When you hit a ball hard, the shutter is open long enough that the ball smears into a faint streak — and the ball-detector, trained on crisp round balls, sees nothing at all. For about half a second after contact, your 4-ball simply didn't exist to the software.

Second: mistaken identity. While the 4-ball was invisible, the cue ball rolled up and stopped where the 4 used to be. The software saw a ball sitting right where it expected the 4 — and assumed it WAS the 4. So the '4' it tracked afterwards was actually the cue ball, and the miss got called on the wrong side. The fix: a resting ball now refuses to become a different-coloured ball. White can't become purple.

Third: the ghost. Even after that fix, the old '4' label stayed stuck at the spot the ball had left, so the real 4 — found again near the pocket — couldn't get its name back. Now a label lets go when its spot is visibly empty, and the real ball reclaims it.

Fourth: the verdict itself. Even with the ball tracked, the app judged the miss from the blurriest instant of the shot. Now it checks something simpler: every glimpse it DID get of the ball lies on one straight line — and a rolling ball can't leave its line and sneak back. So the gap hides nothing, and the verdict is trusted: missed left, 1.3 inches.

entries.title: What the pros do, and what we're borrowing
entries.body: We compared our tracking against published pool-vision systems. Three lessons are now the roadmap.
details: You asked whether fast-ball tracking is a solved problem — it mostly is, and not with expensive cameras. Systems like POOL-AID and PoolLiveAid ran on ordinary webcams a decade ago.

Their trick #1: don't look FOR balls, look for anything that isn't table. A smeared ball doesn't look like a ball, but it never looks like blue felt either. We had this backwards — our smart detector finds balls brilliantly when they're sharp and goes blind when they move. Their approach never goes blind.

Their trick #2: carry uncertainty. When a system loses sight of a ball, it should get less sure about where it is — and search wider — automatically. We'd hand-built a dozen special rules that each approximate a piece of that.

Their trick #3: fit physics to the whole shot. A ball rolls straight, slows smoothly, and bounces off rails at known angles. Fit that model to every glimpse you got, and it fills the gaps — with an honest error bar. That's the plan now, in that order, each step measured before it replaces anything.

entries.title: A first pattern in your misses
entries.body: Among misses the app is confident about, you miss RIGHT about 3x as often as left (25 vs 8). Small sample — a hint, not a diagnosis.
details: Only trusted verdicts are counted — every miss where the app couldn't clearly see the ball is excluded rather than guessed. That keeps the pattern honest, but it also keeps the sample small for now.
As more shots earn trusted verdicts (the physics-fit work in progress), this number firms up. If it holds near 3-to-1, that's the first concrete thing to take to the practice table.

entries.title: The red line is now the real path
entries.body: The 'line it took' overlay draws the ball's entire recorded path — rail bounces included. Nothing is written on top of the video anymore.
details: After a few rounds of your feedback the overlay settled on one principle: draw measurements, not conclusions. The red line is the ball's entire recorded path — rail bounce and all — not a simplified arrow.

Nothing is written on top of the video anymore; the verdict lives in the bar below. The legend drags anywhere and remembers its spot. And a new rule for future changes: overlays get rendered against real footage before they ship, because two of the earlier misses would have been caught by simply looking.

entries.title: Drag the legend out of the way
entries.body: The overlay legend can be dragged anywhere on the video and remembers where you put it — even through rotation.

entries.title: Fast shots keep their trails
entries.body: Hard-hit balls used to vanish from the trails mid-flight. The app now recovers them through the motion blur.
details: A hard-hit ball crosses four of its own widths between frames and smears into a translucent streak. The detector sees nothing — but the pixels still hold the ball.

The recovery: remember what the empty table looks like (the average of the last second and a half), subtract it, and whatever remains that's ball-sized and matches the missing ball's own colour better than any other ball's — that's your ball. It's how your trails now follow the ball all the way to the rail.

One honest limit: a smeared ball's measured position is the middle of the streak, not the ball. Good enough to draw a trail; not good enough to judge a miss by. So recovery feeds the drawings, and verdicts wait for the physics fit.

entries.title: Rotation stays put
entries.body: Rotating the video no longer flips the legend or play button, and toggling overlays no longer un-rotates the video.

entries.title: Honest verdicts
entries.body: When the app can't actually see which side a miss went, it says 'can't tell' instead of guessing.
details: Early on, the app labelled every miss with a side, even when its data was garbage. That's how your miss-left got called miss-right: it measured a direction across a half-second hole and confidently reported nonsense.

The standing rule now: the app only states what it actually measured. When the ball was lost at the decisive moment, the verdict says 'can't tell which side — ball lost after contact' instead of guessing. When it IS sure, that confidence means something.

This matters for the stats. Your miss patterns are only useful if every counted miss is real — one wrong-side label pollutes the pattern more than ten honest abstentions. Trusted verdicts went from 30 to 33 this week, and each 'can't tell' is a known repair target, not a mystery.

entries.title: Sharper shots for free (when you have a minute)
entries.body: One camera dial change — shutter to 1/250 — would make every future recording dramatically easier to analyse. Plain-language walkthrough saved for you.
details: Most of this week's problems trace to motion blur, and most of that traces to shutter speed. Your camera is exposing each frame for about 1/75th of a second; at 1/250th, a hard-hit ball stays a crisp dot instead of a streak.

The full plain-language walkthrough is saved as CAMERA_SETTINGS.md in the project — which dial, which direction, what it costs (a bit of grain, which the software barely notices). No new lighting needed. Whenever you get a minute at the table, it's the single highest-value tweak available.
